extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, and general readers interested in United States administrative law
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying when courts should defer to agency statutory interpretations (Chevron) versus treating them under Skidmore/persuasive-authority, illustrated by United States v. Mead Corp. (2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Administrative implementation of a particular statutory provision qualifies for Chevron deference when it appears that Congress delegated authority to the agency generally to make rules carrying the force of law, and that the agency interpretation claiming deference was promulgated in the exercise of that authority." (Justice Souter)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling Mead formulation: Chevron applies only where there is a congressional delegation of authority to make rules carrying the force of law and the agency interpretation was promulgated in the exercise of that authority. The Court used this standard to limit automatic Chevron deference for many Customs classification decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Mead boundaries of Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Before Mead, it was clear that the Chevron doctrine applied to interpretations adopted in legislative rules and certain formal adjudications, but lower courts differed on whether it also applied to interpretative rules, policy statements, informal adjudications, advisory letters, and amicus briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mead addressed this uncertainty by clarifying that not all agency actions fit within Chevron's scope; whether Chevron applies depends on whether the agency action reflects a delegation to make rules having the force of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Chevron when agency decisions lack force-of-law/precedential character
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing that thousands of tariff decisions are issued each year by the 46 regional offices of the U.S. Customs Service, and that each decision has no precedential value, the Court determined that the Chevron Doctrine should not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency actions that are routine, case-by-case determinations without precedential effect (e.g., regional Customs classification rulings) are unlikely to qualify for Chevron deference because they do not evidence exercise of congressional delegation to make binding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore 'power to persuade' fallback
rubrics_metrics.description: If Chevron deference is not warranted, the agency interpretation may still be entitled to respect according to its 'power to persuade' under Skidmore v. Swift, 323 U.S. 134 (1944).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mead remanded to determine whether the Customs classification decision deserved Skidmore deference. Under Skidmore, courts consider the persuasiveness of the agency's reasoning, consistency, and other factors bearing on its persuasive power (i.e., not entitlement to deference as a matter of law but weight as persuasive authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritativeness as a factor (Scalia's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice Scalia (dissent) believed that Chevron deference should be applied to all agency decisions that are 'authoritative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scalia criticized Mead's reaffirmation of Skidmore as an 'anachronism' and urged a broader application of Chevron to authoritative agency interpretations; this highlights a competing evaluative standard—whether an agency action is sufficiently 'authoritative' to trigger Chevron.
